kept_issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Many tabular data models run CountVectorizer against categorical and text data to featurize the data. At the large scale especially, the `min_df` or `max_features` are commonly used to limit the dimensionality to the most frequent terms. This is important to reduce memory and sometimes may help with generalization of the resulting model.

One problem is that sometimes this long-tail of low-count terms has useful information, and researchers sometimes instead replace these features with a flag indicating that the feature was filtered out. This can further be extended to not only replace it with a single-feature denoting out of dictionary, but a hashbag of N terms denoting the long tail. Eg. a hashbag of 100 terms could be used to denote the long-tail of out of dictionary terms.

### Describe your proposed solution

Update CountVectorizer to enable out-of-dictionary features. Proposed modification stub might be:

```
CountVectorizer(..., out_of_dict_features=1)
```

And docs:
```
    out_of_dict_features : int, default=None
        If not None, will add the specified number of out-of-dictionary
        features. If it is 1, it will add a single feature to denote
        out of dictionary features. If >1, it will add a hashbag of the
        specified size to denote the out of dictionary features. This
        should be used with feature trimming `max_features`, `min_df`,
        and/or `max_df`.
```

Note: I may change this to be the number of bits to use for the out of dict hashbag instead of the feature count.

Example with single out of dictionary feature:
```
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
corpus = [
    'This is the first document test.',
    'This document is the second document.',
    'And this is the third one.',
    'Is this the first document?',
]

vectorizer = CountVectorizer(analyzer='word', ngram_range=(1, 1), min_df=2, out_of_dict_features=1)
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(corpus)

print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print(X.toarray())
```

Mock output:
```
['document' 'first' 'is' 'the' 'this' '<out_of_dict_0>']
[[1 1 1 1 1 1]
 [2 0 1 1 1 1]
 [0 0 1 1 1 3]
 [1 1 1 1 1 0]]
```
The last column in the above is the count of out-of-dictionary features.

Example with multiple out-of-dict features:
```
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
corpus = [
    'This is the first document test.',
    'This document is the second document.',
    'And this is the third one.',
    'Is this the first document?',
]

vectorizer = CountVectorizer(analyzer='word', ngram_range=(1, 1), min_df=2, out_of_dict_features=100)
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(corpus)

print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print(X.toarray())
```

Mock output:
```
['document' 'first' 'is' 'the' 'this' '<out_of_dict_79>']
[[1 1 1 1 1 <100x bag count of out of dictionary features appended>]
 [2 0 1 1 1 <100x bag count of out of dictionary features appended>]
 [0 0 1 1 1 <100x bag count of out of dictionary features appended>]
 [1 1 1 1 1 <100x bag count of out of dictionary features appended>]]
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

This is difficult to implement in production without this change where you don't know some of the never-seen out of dictionary terms that it may be inferenced against.

### Additional context

I'm starting to code a PR to add this feature. Let me know if there is any feedback, requests, or comments!
kept_issues.title: CountVectorizer out of dictionary features

kept_issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

The `cv_results_` dictionary generated by `sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV` and `sklearn.model_selection.RandomizedSearchCV` only has a key `rank_test_<score_name>` to show ranking of the best parameter candidate but this rank is sometimes misguiding.

Example (Taken from the skikit-learn documentation of `sklearn.model_selection.GridSearchCV`):-
>>> from sklearn import svm, datasets
>>> from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
>>> iris = datasets.load_iris()
>>> parameters = {'kernel':('linear', 'rbf'), 'C':[1, 10]}
>>> svc = svm.SVC()
>>> clf = GridSearchCV(svc, parameters)
>>> clf.fit(iris.data, iris.target)

Keys `mean_test_score` and `rank_test_score` of `clf.cv_results_` dictionary shows the following output:

![scikit-learn](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20677278/144740114-c93d769d-06f1-4b5d-b204-e27e2dcc00c8.JPG)

However if we enable the parameter `return_train_score = TRUE` during training we can see that `clf.best_params_` returns the parameter candidate that has the least **difference** between `mean_train_score` and `mean_test_score`, therefore in cases like this `rank_test_score` does not signify which parameter candidate is the best.

So if we can add a new key named **'difference'** that will signify the difference between the `mean_train_score` and `mean_test_score` then we can get a **better perspective** of which parameter candidate was choosen  to be the best in cases like this. 
Example:-
![scikit-learn_2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20677278/144741020-4078b741-50f2-4581-b6ee-6fd4df798781.JPG)



### Describe your proposed solution

The key `difference = abs('mean_train_<score_name>' - 'mean_test_<score_name>')`
we can add the key to the dictionary `results` inside the function `_store` 

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b1202af3b379e698539a2719f2b1e28706ce5388/sklearn/model_selection/_search.py#L953

This should also work in case of '**multimetric**' scenario.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

- we can name the key something else like '**error**' (suggestions are welcome!).
- we can remove the `abs()` method and keep the real difference values.

### Additional context

If the suggested enhancement is accepted by the core devs I would like to implement it
kept_issues.title: 'cv_results_' dictionary should also have a 'difference' key when 'return_train_score = TRUE'

This is a follow-up of #9913. The following code is expected to fail with unshuffled cross-validation since `SVC` cannot be fit with a single class.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X,y = make_classification(n_classes=3,  n_informative=6,  shuffle=False)

svc = SVC()
svc.fit(X,y)

# Error occurs here
train_sizes, train_scores, test_scores = learning_curve(svc, X, y, cv=10)
```

Since we have `error_score=np.nan`, we do not raise an error but instead output `nan`. This is the expected behaviour.
However, we could improve a bit more the user experience by adding a warning as done in `GridSearchCV` for instance to indicate the failures on the CV folds.
kept_issues.title: Raise warning when fit/score fail in learning curve

Describe the workflow you want to enable

Computing a net benefit curve in support of decision curve analysis. 

See [1] for primary publication (2,301 citations on google scholar) and [2] for publication on usage and interpretation (148 citations in google scholar).

1. Vickers, Andrew J., and Elena B. Elkin. "Decision curve analysis: a novel method for evaluating prediction models." Medical Decision Making 26.6 (2006): 565-574.
2. Vickers, Andrew J., Ben van Calster, and Ewout W. Steyerberg. "A simple, step-by-step guide to interpreting decision curve analysis." Diagnostic and prognostic research 3.1 (2019): 1-8.
3. (edit by @lorentzenchr)

 Describe your proposed solution

Given predicted likelihoods and ground truth labels, produce 'net benefit' over a configurable decision threshold cut-points:

 

Where p_t is the likelihood threshold for considering the prediction a positive (e.g. {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, ..., 1.}) 

I could see this feature being implemented similarly to calibration curves - methods to produce the raw net benefit data and possibly additional functions to plot it.

I have an implementation that isn't public yet and I'm open to working on a PR to get this into sklearn if the community is interested. I'd also be open to a 'contrib' package.

 Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

Some code exists in other languages to produce these curves and subsequent plots, but I'm not aware of a well-maintained Python implementation.

 Additional context

_(I would suggest reading citation 2 above for more thorough explanation and examples - see the later examples for common questions)_

Net benefit is primarily for assessing models that are intended to aid an individual in making a decision. 

For example, given a model for the likelihood of rain later in the day: what level of certainty do you need to pack a jacket/umbrella? If you are risk averse, you may decide that even a 5% chance of rain is enough motivation. Or in contrast, another user may be risk tolerant and would need 75% chance of rain to warrant rain gear.

A net benefit curve accounts for both calibration and classification performance, helping users understand the value of using the model versus always acting a specific way. Given a net benefit curve and it's comparison to naively "treating all" or "treating none":

- The risk averse user may find that the model has higher net-benefit than always wearing a coat (i.e. treat all) for their 5% threshold. This user would then only prepare for rain if the model's output was above 5%.
- Instead, the risk tolerant user may find that there is little net benefit to relying on the model for their 75% threshold, and they will have the same net benefit if they simply ignore the model and never bring an umbrella (i.e. treat none). 

Net benefit is in units of true positives is in the range (-inf, true positive rate]. Negative values indicate harm and that it is better to assume no positives at that threshold (i.e. treat none) rather than rely on the model.

Describe the workflow you want to enable

I am writing a pipeline that automates training and taking metrics over various classifications/clusterings of the data. I would like the user to be able to specify the metric function(s) from sklearn.metrics. However, as the module currently stands, not all metrics accept the same standard set of args. Some are supervised, and only take y_true, y_pred or labels_true,labels_pred. Others are unsupervised and accept only labels_pred, X. Still others only consume what they need, say for instance labels_pred,X, but accept kwargs, so one could call metrics.nice_function(y_true=Y_true, y_pred=Y_pred, X=X,foo=bar) and the function will still run, only using what it needs.

 Describe your proposed solution

Add kwargs to every function signature in sklearn.metrics. Also, it may be nice if the clustering kwargs are changed to y_true, y_pred to match the classification functions.

 Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The workaround right now is to have the user pass lambda functions that wrap the function they want. However, this 1) is an extra step that could be solved by a standard API, 2) removes all function context variables like .__name__, you can't tell what the user is really calling - i use __name__ to build the keys of a metrics dictionary that holds the outputs of the requested metrics.

 Additional context

I intend to author a PR in the coming week that standardizes the metrics interface.
kept_issues.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

I am writing a pipeline that automates training and taking metrics over various classifications/clusterings of the data. I would like the user to be able to specify the metric function(s) from `sklearn.metrics`. However, as the module currently stands, not all metrics accept the same standard set of args. Some are supervised, and only take `y_true, y_pred` or `labels_true,labels_pred`. Others are unsupervised and accept only `labels_pred, X`. Still others only consume what they need, say for instance `labels_pred,X`, but accept `**kwargs`, so one could call `metrics.nice_function(y_true=Y_true, y_pred=Y_pred, X=X,foo=bar)` and the function will still run, only using what it needs.

### Describe your proposed solution

Add `**kwargs` to every function signature in `sklearn.metrics`. Also, it may be nice if the clustering kwargs are changed to `y_true, y_pred` to match the classification functions.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

The workaround right now is to have the user pass lambda functions that wrap the function they want. However, this 1) is an extra step that could be solved by a standard API, 2) removes all function context variables like `.__name__`, you can't tell what the user is really calling - i use `__name__` to build the keys of a metrics dictionary that holds the outputs of the requested metrics.

### Additional context

I intend to author a PR in the coming week that standardizes the `metrics` interface.
kept_issues.title: Standardize sklearn.metrics args
